name: Natural Language and Speech
guide:
Natural language and speech engineering means building the systems that let software understand, generate, or transcribe human language and voice. In practice that covers automatic speech recognition, text to speech, conversational voice agents, and the natural language processing layers behind chatbots and voice assistants. This work is distinct from general machine learning engineering, which more often means building and shipping model pipelines across any data type, and from AI research, which is judged on new methods and papers rather than production systems. People confuse the three because job titles blend them freely. Our own sample shows titles like Senior Machine Learning Engineer, Voice Agents sitting next to Research Engineer, Audio and Speech for what is functionally similar work.

Day to day, an NLP or speech engineer spends more time than a general MLE on audio pipelines, tokenization for spoken language, latency budgets for real time voice, and evaluation of transcription or dialogue quality rather than pure model accuracy. A research-leaning speech role, like the Research Engineer and Staff Research Engineer, Voice and Speech postings we see from Decagon, still ships toward a product rather than only a publication. That is the practical line between this discipline and AI research, even when a title says research engineer. Product and program roles also live in this category in our data, including product managers for voice AI at ServiceNow and Hopper, because voice product decisions require the same domain fluency as the engineering side.

Formal credentials in our sample are hard to pin down because most postings do not list a degree requirement explicitly. Where seniority points to research adjacent roles, such as the staff research scientist and research engineer titles at companies like DeepL and Decagon, a graduate degree in computational linguistics, speech processing, or machine learning is a common informal expectation, though we cannot confirm that directly from these listings. Certifications essentially do not appear in this data at all. Across all 23 postings and their listed skills, not one names a vendor certification, so anyone marketing a speech or NLP certificate should treat it as a resume add-on rather than a hiring requirement here.

Seniority in our sample skews upward. Of 23 open postings, none are labeled entry level or junior, nine are Senior, five are Staff, four are Manager, three are Mid-level, and one is Lead. That pattern suggests companies are hiring speech and NLP talent to lead specific systems, such as voice agents, ASR pipelines, or dialogue models, rather than to staff a growing junior bench. What gets someone hired at the mid to senior level, based on the roles here, is direct experience shipping a speech or conversational system end to end, not just NLP coursework or a general ML background.

The named tools in our skills data lean heavily on Python and PyTorch, which appear across nearly every technical posting, with Rust showing up often enough to be notable for performance-sensitive audio and inference work. Large Language Models and Transformers are named skills on multiple postings, alongside more specialized mentions of CUDA, Triton, JAX, TensorFlow, and Hugging Face for model training and serving. Infrastructure skills appear too, including AWS, Docker, and Kubernetes, reflecting that these roles often own deployment as well as modeling. A smaller number of postings name Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Reinforcement Learning, Fine-tuning, and Model Evaluation, which point to the applied research end of the discipline rather than pure infrastructure work.

As of our most recent data pull, we currently track approximately 15 open postings in Natural Language and Speech that were live on the last day we scanned, out of 23 total postings gathered for this category. Salary data is thin. Only 2 of the 23 postings carry a listed salary range, both for a Senior Machine Learning Engineer, Voice Assistant role at Roku, ranging from $128,573 to $139,162 per year. That is not enough data to state a market range for the discipline as a whole, so we report it narrowly as what those two Roku postings show rather than as a general benchmark.

The companies appearing most often in our current sample are Decagon with three postings, followed by Deepgram, Together AI, ServiceNow, Roku, and DeepL with two each. The rest of the roles are spread across single postings at companies including Hugging Face, GitLab, Datadog, Cresta, Baseten, Sierra, Observe.AI, Spotify, Hopper, and Jupus. This is a live snapshot from our own job tracking database, not a broad labor market claim, and it will shift as postings age out or new ones are added. Anyone using this guide to plan a job search should treat it as a current signal from theworldofai.org's own data rather than a permanent statement about the field.

reading.body:
Voice AI hiring is concentrated among infrastructure and platform companies rather than consumer applications, with roles emphasizing production-grade systems over research.

The companies posting these roles split into two groups. Infrastructure plays like Deepgram, Baseten, and Together AI are hiring for inference runtimes and agent frameworks. Enterprise software firms like ServiceNow, Datadog, and Cresta are building voice into existing products. Consumer-facing companies appear only as outliers. Deepgram, a speech-to-text platform, has posted the most openings. This pattern suggests voice AI has moved past the model development phase into embedding within systems that need to run at scale.

The seniority levels are high. Most roles are senior engineer, staff engineer, or manager tier. The job titles emphasize agents, voice experience, and inference rather than foundational model training. This reflects that production voice systems require infrastructure expertise as much as model expertise. Salary data is sparse, but two Roku postings show compensation around $128k-$139k annually, placing these as mid-level technical roles rather than peak-tier AI researcher positions.

Geography splits between US tech hubs and remote work. San Francisco concentrates infrastructure roles. London, Bangalore, and Paris appear once each. Five of seventeen roles are explicitly remote. The data does not cover hiring volume trends, how these postings correlate with actual hiring, or whether voice AI hiring is growing relative to other AI specializations.
